The basket boats of Ngan Ha

If you are fortunate enough to visit the village of Ngan Ha, on the south-central coast of Vietnam, you might notice large round shapes scattered along the shoreline. At first glance, they could easily be mistaken for giant turtle shells. Look more closely, though, and you'll discover they are actually enormous woven baskets - and, remarkably, these baskets are also boats. Known locally as thuyen thung, these basket boats can be found in fishing villages all along Vietnam's coastline.

The story behind these unusual boats is almost as fascinating as the boats themselves, combining cleverness with a healthy dose of tax avoidance. During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when Vietnam was under French colonial rule, the French authorities taxed a long list of goods, boats included. For villages like Ngan Ha, where fishing was the main source of income, this tax threatened people's livelihoods. To get around it, local fishermen designed a new kind of vessel that could technically be called a basket rather than a boat. Since baskets weren't taxed, the fishermen of Ngan Ha and other coastal villages could keep fishing without paying a cent.

The boats themselves are woven from thin strips of bamboo that have been dried in the sun. Once woven into the traditional round shape, they're coated with several layers of a plant-based waterproofing material called chai. If the boat ever springs a leak, fixing it is simple: just add another layer of chai.

Steering a thuyen thung takes practice, and can be a real challenge for the uninitiated, as well as entertaining for those watching - it takes a while to work out how to paddle one without spinning in useless circles. Local villagers, however, grow up around these boats and learn to handle them with ease from a young age.

What began as a clever way to dodge an unfair tax has become something else entirely for many coastal communities today. Tourists now travel specifically to see the basket boats of villages like Ngan Ha, and the more adventurous visitors even take one out for a spin themselves.

Kryson crouched low in the shadow of Troy's massive stone walls, silently going over his lines one more time. Everything depended on whether he could convince the Trojans that the Greek army had truly given up their ten-year siege and sailed home at last.

He glanced sideways at the enormous wooden horse the crafty Greeks had built and left standing just outside the city gates. Somewhere inside its huge hollow belly, his fellow soldiers were waiting in the heat and the dark. He didn't envy them.

Eventually a few curious Trojans noticed the strange wooden structure and crept closer to investigate. For the first time in a decade, the Greek camp beyond the walls stood completely empty and silent. Was the war really over? And what exactly was this towering horse supposed to mean? Taking a breath, Kryson stepped out of hiding and began his carefully rehearsed story.

'Please, spare me!' he cried out. 'My own countrymen abandoned me when they sailed for home. They've finally accepted they could never conquer Troy. This horse was built as a gift - an offering to your city's strength, left behind as a token of respect.'

Exhausted after years of war, the Trojans were easily won over by Kryson's dramatic performance. Desperate to believe their enemy had truly given up, they decided to haul the horse inside the city walls as a trophy of their victory.

Not everyone was convinced. A handful of Trojans eyed the strange wooden creature with unease and argued against bringing it inside at all, but their warnings were drowned out by the noise of celebration. Thick ropes were tied to the horse, and crowds of excited citizens pushed forward, each eager for the honour of helping pull it through the gates.

And so, without realising it, the Trojans dragged their own enemy straight into the heart of their city. Once night fell, the hidden soldiers climbed down from inside the horse, threw open the gates, and let in the waiting Greek army. Troy fell that same night. Ever since, the phrase 'wooden horse' has come to describe any gift that looks beguiling but ultimately leads to disaster.

Subject: Thank you!
Attached: photo1.jpg

Dear Grandpa,

I hope your back is feeling better and that the physio is helping. I know how much you hate sitting still too. Thank you so much for my birthday card and the gift voucher - it arrived in the letterbox right on the morning of my birthday!

It's such a shame you weren't well enough to come to my birthday dinner. It was such a fun night and I really think you would have loved it.

Mum and Dad took me to Sabor, the new Brazilian restaurant near the cinema. At this restaurant, you actually get a little card with a green side and a red side! Imagine that, Grandpa. I promise it's not as strange as it sounds.

Sabor is a churrascaria, which means waiters walk around with huge skewers of grilled meat and carve pieces straight onto your plate. You flip your card to green when you want more, and red when you need a break. I kept mine on green for most of the night. We started with garlic bread and cheese rolls (your favourite kind of bread) and then the skewers started arriving. When the waiter carved the first skewer right at our table, sparks from the grill actually floated past us in the air. He must have noticed my face because he laughed and told me the sparks were completely normal, just part of the show.

And then came the best part, Grandpa. After the meat, they brought out a huge bowl of grilled pineapple with cinnamon sugar, and our waiter, Mateus, challenged Dad and me to see who could flip a piece into their mouth first. I missed every single time. Dad, of course, caught his on the very first try. He said he'd had 'years of secret practice.' By the end there was pineapple juice absolutely everywhere.

Next Mateus brought around little bowls of spicy sauce and dared us to guess the secret ingredient before he'd tell us (it was passionfruit, in case you were wondering). I had SUCH a good night, Grandpa. I know you'll be worrying about my shirt, but they actually gave us bibs shaped like little capes when we sat down, so I stayed completely clean. I had a wonderful time. Maybe we could all go back together for your birthday next month?

Bye for now.

Love,
Priya :)

Limestone caves

Caves can form in regions where the ground contains layers of limestone rock. Limestone is a soluble sedimentary rock, meaning it can gradually be dissolved. It forms mainly from the build-up of marine animal remains, such as coral, over enormous stretches of time. As water filters underground through cracks in the limestone over millions of years, it can slowly carve out underground channels, and sometimes truly spectacular caves.

It isn't only the flow of water through these cracks that shapes caves, though - the acidity of that water plays a major role too. When rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide, both from the atmosphere and from the soil it passes through, it forms a weak acid known as carbonic acid. As this slightly acidic water trickles underground through cracks and fissures, it gradually dissolves the surrounding limestone. Along with hollowing out caves, this same process may also create striking rock formations, such as stalactites and stalagmites.

The following investigation is designed to demonstrate what happens to a soluble material when water flows over it continuously.

Investigation materials
- 3 blocks of salt
- a jug to hold the water
- a piece of cloth or towel
- large rubber bands
- a large plastic tub
- a handful of small stones

Investigation steps
1. Place one salt block into the tub. Prop up one end using the stones, so only one edge rests on the base of the tub.
2. Place the other two salt blocks side by side, on their longest side. Wrap rubber bands around them to hold them together, then set them on top of the first block already in the tub.
3. Place a cloth into a jug of water, with one end hanging out over the side. Slowly tilt the jug and cloth so that water drips steadily onto the top of the two stacked salt blocks - a few drops per minute works well. Let it drip overnight.
4. Remove the rubber bands and separate the blocks to reveal the 'cave' that has formed.

Mateo's Secret

'Mateo! Come on, we need someone who actually knows how to play goalkeeper!' I yelled.

'Can't today! I've got something to do,' he shouted back, still walking steadily down the long dirt track that led nowhere useful at all. The village shops were the other way entirely, and as far as I knew, this track only led through the forest before eventually reaching the lake.

'But it won't take long,' I said. 'Just twenty minutes! They're destroying us, it's four-nil already, we really need you,' I pleaded, jogging to catch up with him. It was completely unlike Mateo to skip a game of football. What was going on with him?

'Where are you even going?' I asked, falling into step beside him.

'It's just...' Mateo started, glancing back over his shoulder at the other boys, who weren't paying us any attention at all. 'You can come, if you want,' he whispered. 'It's not far from here.'

I don't know exactly why, but suddenly my curiosity was aroused. Mateo lived and breathed football; there was nothing else he'd ever choose over a match. I knew my friend was hiding something.

'I might come along for a bit,' I said, trying to sound casual and hide how curious I actually was.

We walked in silence for a few minutes until Mateo pointed to a gap in the bushes at the side of the track, and we pushed through into the forest itself. The air cooled almost instantly as the sunlight vanished behind the thick green canopy above us. There was no proper path here, but the flattened undergrowth made it obvious that someone had come this way recently.

'So where exactly are we going?' I eventually asked.

'We're nearly there,' he said. 'We need to stay really quiet from here. No sudden movements, okay? We don't want to scare them off.' He shifted a bag over his shoulder that I hadn't even noticed he was carrying. As the plants grew thicker, we needed both hands just to push through the leaves and vines.

Soon we were crawling, boxed in on every side by the undergrowth pressing close around us. My heart was pounding, and I couldn't tell if it was from the effort or from nerves.

'Okay,' Mateo whispered, and as the plants finally opened into a small clearing, I realised I'd been holding my breath the whole time. Thin beams of light broke through from somewhere above, and as my eyes adjusted, I saw we weren't alone. Mateo was already digging through his bag, pulling out scraps of bread and dried meat. Almost immediately, several small furry shapes came scurrying out from every direction towards his offerings.

'There's four of them,' Mateo said quietly. 'Their mum got hurt and can't hunt properly yet, but she's getting stronger every day.'

Why it's cool to be kind

Every morning on the way to school, my dad and I stop at the same small bakery and buy breakfast: a ham and cheese roll for him, and a cheese and spinach roll for me. Last Tuesday, though, Dad bought three rolls instead of two - one for him, one for me, and one for the man who sits outside the train station every morning. I hope he enjoyed it as much as I enjoyed watching Dad hand it over. Giving felt good; being kind felt good.

Scientific research into kindness shows that it benefits human wellbeing in several different ways at once: the person performing a kind act feels happier and more positive, and the person receiving it benefits directly too. Interestingly, people who simply witness an act of kindness from a distance also experience a kind of secondhand happiness boost, similar to what the person who acted kindly feels. Kindness tends to spread through communities this way - one small act can inspire several more.

In effect, being kind stretches our thinking beyond ourselves. To act kindly towards someone, we first have to notice them and their situation - to think about what a stranger sitting outside a train station might actually need, for example. Recognising someone's need and doing something about it makes the receiver feel seen and valued, while the giver usually ends up feeling happier, more connected, and less alone.

While kindness can sometimes seem like a very grown-up habit, researchers suggest it's worth actively encouraging in children too. Very young children tend to be naturally generous, but somewhere between infancy and the middle years of primary school, many kids start focusing more on themselves than on others.

One research project studying children aged 9 to 11 looked specifically at how performing small acts of kindness affected their happiness. Over several weeks, one group of children carried out three kind acts each week for people of their choosing, while another group simply kept track of three enjoyable places they visited each week. Just like similar research involving adults, the children who performed acts of kindness reported greater happiness and satisfaction than those who only visited pleasant places. Kids who initiated their own acts of kindness also became noticeably more popular and accepted among their classmates.

Humans have an enormous capacity for kindness, and it's something deeply built into how our societies function - caring for one another has likely helped our species survive this long. In our busy modern lives, we probably just need the occasional reminder that being kind, at any age, is a genuinely cool thing to do.

Why it's cool to be kind

Every morning on the way to school, my dad and I stop at the same small bakery and buy breakfast: a ham and cheese roll for him, and a cheese and spinach roll for me. Last Tuesday, though, Dad bought three rolls instead of two - one for him, one for me, and one for the man who sits outside the train station every morning. I hope he enjoyed it as much as I enjoyed watching Dad hand it over. Giving felt good; being kind felt good.

Scientific research into kindness shows that it benefits human wellbeing in several different ways at once: the person performing a kind act feels happier and more positive, and the person receiving it benefits directly too.
